<!-- slide · dimred divider -->
# Dimensionality Reduction {.divider}

[Many features into two axes · Day 01]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide · dimred theory 1 -->
## Why Reduce, and Which Method {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Three projections, three jobs

Genomic data is wide: thousands of genes, hundreds of samples. You can't see 5000 dimensions, so you **project** to two while keeping what matters. The three standard tools keep different things, so they answer different questions.

| Method | Keeps | Speed | Best genomics use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PCA** | Global variance, real distances, interpretable axes | Fast | Population structure from genotypes/ancestry; bulk RNA-seq QC; batch detection |
| **t-SNE** | Local neighbourhoods (tight clusters) | Slow | Single-cell RNA-seq cluster visualisation |
| **UMAP** | Local + some global; reproducible | Fast | Single-cell (the scanpy default); large datasets |

The rule of thumb: **PCA to understand structure and distances, t-SNE / UMAP to see clusters.**


<!-- slide · dimred theory 2 -->
## The Three Rules That Save You {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Before you trust an embedding

**PCA is linear; t-SNE and UMAP are not.** PCA axes are combinations of features you can interpret and whose distances are real. In t-SNE and UMAP, **distances between clusters carry no meaning**, only "these points are neighbours."

**Run t-SNE / UMAP on PCA-reduced data.** For thousands of genes, reduce to ~50 PCs first, then embed. It is faster and denoises. (Our ancestry data is already 5-dimensional, so we skip that here.)

**Seed everything.** t-SNE and UMAP are stochastic; set `random_state` or the picture changes every run.


<!-- slide · dimred data -->
## Dim. Reduction · The Data {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction]{.eyebrow}

### Real ancestry: 120 individuals, 5 populations

`load_admixture()` gives each individual's ancestry split across five source populations (`K1`–`K5`, summing to 1) plus the population label. This is the textbook home of PCA in genomics: **revealing population structure**.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()   # individual, population, K1..K5
adm.head(4)
```


<!-- slide · pca step 1 -->
## PCA · Step 1 — Project {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction · PCA]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Scale, fit, plot

Scale each feature, fit PCA, and scatter the first two components. Structure is already visible, but we can't yet tell which cluster is which.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "7-9,12"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)            # centre + scale each feature
pca = PCA(n_components=5, random_state=42)
coords = pca.fit_transform(Xs)                    # project onto components

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
ax.scatter(coords[:, 0], coords[:, 1], color=GREY, s=24, alpha=.7, linewidths=0)
ax.set_xlabel("PC1"); ax.set_ylabel("PC2")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · pca step 2 -->
## PCA · Step 2 — Colour by Population {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction · PCA]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Structure appears

Colour by population and add the variance each axis explains. The five groups separate, and PCA's real distances show **AMR sitting between the others**, it is the admixed population.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "10-11,14-18"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
pca = PCA(n_components=5, random_state=42)
coords = pca.fit_transform(Xs)
var = pca.explained_variance_ratio_ * 100         # % variance per PC
pal = {"EUR": GREEN, "AFR": BLUE, "EAS": AMBER, "SAS": RED, "AMR": PURPLE}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
for p, c in pal.items():
    m = adm.population == p
    ax.scatter(coords[m, 0], coords[m, 1], color=c, s=24, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=.3, label=p)
ax.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({var[0]:.0f}%)"); ax.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({var[1]:.0f}%)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, title="population")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · pca scree -->
## PCA · How Many Components? {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction · PCA]{.eyebrow}

### The scree plot, and a compositional quirk

The scree plot shows variance per component. Normally you look for an "elbow." Here you get **four near-equal components and a fifth at zero**: because the five fractions sum to 1, the data really lives in four dimensions.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "9-10,14-16"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
pca = PCA(n_components=5, random_state=42).fit(Xs)
var = pca.explained_variance_ratio_ * 100
cum = var.cumsum()                                # cumulative variance

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
pcs = range(1, 6)
ax.bar(pcs, var, color=GREEN, alpha=.85, edgecolor="white")   # per-PC variance
ax.plot(pcs, cum, color=INK, marker="o", lw=1.5)              # cumulative
ax.set_xlabel("principal component"); ax.set_ylabel("variance explained (%)")
ax.set_title("4 even PCs, PC5 ≈ 0 (fractions sum to 1)", color="#333333")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · tsne -->
## t-SNE · Local Clusters {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction · t-SNE]{.eyebrow}

### Same data, tightened into clusters

t-SNE drops the linear constraint and pulls neighbours together. The populations become tight, well-separated blobs, great for *spotting* clusters, but the gaps between them mean nothing.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4,9"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
emb = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=42).fit_transform(Xs)

pal = {"EUR": GREEN, "AFR": BLUE, "EAS": AMBER, "SAS": RED, "AMR": PURPLE}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
for p, c in pal.items():
    m = adm.population == p
    ax.scatter(emb[m, 0], emb[m, 1], color=c, s=24, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=.3, label=p)
ax.set_xlabel("t-SNE 1"); ax.set_ylabel("t-SNE 2")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · umap -->
## UMAP · Local + Some Global {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction · UMAP]{.eyebrow}

### Faster, reproducible, the single-cell default

UMAP keeps tight clusters like t-SNE but runs faster and preserves a little more of the global layout. `n_neighbors` trades local detail for global structure; `min_dist` controls how tightly points pack.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4,9"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import umap

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
emb = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, random_state=42).fit_transform(Xs)

pal = {"EUR": GREEN, "AFR": BLUE, "EAS": AMBER, "SAS": RED, "AMR": PURPLE}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
for p, c in pal.items():
    m = adm.population == p
    ax.scatter(emb[m, 0], emb[m, 1], color=c, s=24, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=.3, label=p)
ax.set_xlabel("UMAP 1"); ax.set_ylabel("UMAP 2")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · dimred comparison -->
## Side by Side {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction]{.eyebrow}

### Same ancestry data, three projections

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
import umap

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
pca_emb = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=42).fit_transform(Xs)
tsne_emb = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=42).fit_transform(Xs)
umap_emb = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, random_state=42).fit_transform(Xs)

pal = {"EUR": GREEN, "AFR": BLUE, "EAS": AMBER, "SAS": RED, "AMR": PURPLE}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 4.2))
for ax, emb, title in zip(axes, [pca_emb, tsne_emb, umap_emb], ["PCA", "t-SNE", "UMAP"]):
    for p, c in pal.items():
        m = adm.population == p
        ax.scatter(emb[m, 0], emb[m, 1], color=c, s=20, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=.3, label=p)
    ax.set_title(title, fontweight="bold", color="#333333")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="best")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
**PCA** keeps real distances and interpretable axes, reach for it first and for population structure. **t-SNE** and **UMAP** trade distance for crisp clusters, reach for them on single-cell. Same five populations here, three different lenses.
:::

<!-- slide · umap as network -->
## UMAP Is a Network {.smaller}

[Dimensionality reduction · UMAP]{.eyebrow}

### The embedding is a neighbour graph laid flat

UMAP works in two moves: first it builds a weighted **k-nearest-neighbour graph** (who is close to whom), then it lays that graph out in 2D. `umap.plot.connectivity` draws the graph itself, points plus the edges. Dense clumps are the populations (everyone is everyone's neighbour); the thin threads between clumps are the handful of cross-population links. Seeing the graph explains *why* UMAP clusters: it is a network embedding, not a projection.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "3,8,9"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.8
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import umap, umap.plot

adm = load_admixture()
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values)

reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, random_state=42).fit(Xs)   # .fit keeps the model
umap.plot.connectivity(reducer, show_points=True)   # draw the neighbour graph
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
UMAP first builds a **kNN graph**, then embeds it. `connectivity` shows that graph directly: tight knots are clusters, thin bridges are the rare links between them. The 2D scatter you usually see is just this network, flattened.
:::
